findings.title: The switch that 'closes the loop' does not exist as an object: no lever, no on/off state, nothing to look at
findings.problem: The Playground's only electrical lesson (per docs and R4B: 'a switch closes the loop') is taught by a text prompt, not by a thing. No switch mesh exists anywhere in the room. decor.ts playground() builds a lamp post, a bulb sphere and a socket box, but no switch (grep 'switch' in src/levels/decor.ts, dressing.ts, src/render, src/props finds nothing). The 'switch' is an invisible 1.9 m radius around switchAt (7.55,-6.35), which is just the lamp post's base (game.ts:244 nearSwitch; level switchAt in playground.ts:6). Pressing E flips the boolean `switchedOn` and spawns 6 sparks (game.ts:217). The only way to know the switch state is to read the prompt pill. Shot 14 shows 'E Switch on (needs power first)'. Shot 15, after pressing E, shows the identical scene, with only the pill changed to 'E Switch it off'. In shot 24 (HUD hidden, plugged in, switch off) a first-time viewer cannot tell why the lamp is dark, or that a switch is involved at all. This breaks DR-26 (the concept must be a physical act on an object, not a prompt) and DR-47 (device state shown on the device). It also breaks DR-37: the open switch is a hidden rule, because the player plugs in, sees nothing happen, and has to read the card to learn that a switch exists. A learner leaves without having seen a switch open or close a gap, which is the one idea the room claims to teach.
evidence: src/levels/decor.ts:83-120 (playground decor: lamp, bulb, socket; no switch mesh)
findings.fix:
In decor.ts playground(), add a chunky wall-box-style rocker or toggle switch on the lamp post at about (t.x+.55, 1.05, t.z-.35+.12), facing the approach (towards −x/+z):
- A housing rbox(.22,.32,.12,.03) in INK-outline neutral (#f0ece2), with a lever box(.07,.16,.06) in job yellow #ffc629.
- The lever rotates +0.45 rad (ON) / −0.45 rad (OFF).
- A small 'I/O' decal, or a red OFF / green ON pip (MeshBasicMaterial, unlit).

Return the lever from Decor (e.g. `decor.switchLever`). In game.ts, set `lever.rotation.x = switchedOn ? .45 : -.45` whenever switchedOn changes (game.ts:217), with a 60 ms snap tween and the existing click sound.

Optionally draw the lamp's own cord as a TubeGeometry from the socket box (t.x,.2,t.z) up into the post base, with the switch visibly on that line, so the 'loop' runs socket → switch → bulb. Move switchAt to the lever, so the E radius centres on a visible object.
findings.verify: New screenshots: zoom 9 at the lamp with the HUD hidden (CSS through g.page), before and after E, with and without the plug. A viewer can name ON/OFF from the lever alone. Add a Playwright assertion that snapshot().switchedOn flips, and a unit or DOM-free check that the lever's rotation.x sign follows it. Retake playground-teach-15 and -24.
findings.verify_reason: Grepping src/ for switch, lever and toggle finds no switch mesh anywhere. decor.ts:83-114 builds only the post, shade, bulb sphere and socket. nearSwitch (game.ts:244) is a 1.9 m radius around switchAt (7.55,-6.35, playground.ts:6). That point is exactly the lamp post's centre: lamp group at t.x+.55, t.z-.35 (decor.ts:89). E only flips the boolean and spawns 6 sparks (game.ts:217). I reproduced it: verify-01 (pill 'Switch on (needs power first)') and verify-02 (after E, pill 'Switch it off') show the same scene, and only the pill text changes. mockups/review4/DESIGN_B.md:214 states the room's teaching value is 'that a switch closes the loop', so the one taught concept has no object, which breaks DR-26 and DR-47.
extra_evidence: mockups/review4/DESIGN_B.md:214 ('that a switch closes the loop')

findings.title: The lamp lights only as part of win(): the cause→effect beat can't be observed or repeated and is buried under confetti and the card
findings.problem:
The lamp's lit state isn't driven by the circuit. decor.ts lightUp() (decor.ts:93) is called only from Game.win() (game.ts:350). The circuit tick wins the instant loads[0] turns 'on' (game.ts:348). Three consequences:

1. The player can never see the core relationship 'switch closed + plug in → lamp on; switch open → lamp off'. There's no off again and no second try, so experimenting is impossible.
2. The moment the loop closes, confetti (90 at the lamp head plus 40 over Pip) and the win push-in fire in the same frame. The result card covers the right half of the screen about 1 s later.
   - Shot 25 (first frame after E, HUD hidden): the lamp head is already hidden in a confetti cloud.
   - Shot 16 (switch first, then plug in): Pip cheers in confetti at the instant of plugging, so the plug-in itself is the win and the switch is never seen to matter.
   - Shots 09–11: the card is up and covers the scene while the lamp has been lit for under a second.
3. The current pulses, which are the room's only 'current flows now' signal, get about 1 s on screen before the card.

This breaks DR-28 (consequence first, readable, then the message), DR-26 (the concept must be manipulable), and DR-11 (the success beat should frame the working machine, not hide it). For a tutorial, the payoff of the lesson is reduced to a flash.
findings.fix:
Decouple the lamp from winning:
1. Return `setLit(on:boolean)` from the playground Decor instead of the one-shot lightUp. Lit = the hot bulb material, the glow and the pointLamp visible. Unlit restores toon('#6b6f84') and hides the glow and light.
2. Each tick in game.ts:348, call `decor.setLit(this.circuit.loads[0].state==='on')`.
3. Replace the instant win with a dwell. Add a field `litFor`:
   - while the load is on, `litFor+=dt`, else `litFor=0`;
   - call `win()` when `litFor>=1.2`.
4. In win(), keep the confetti but delay the result card by about 0.8 s (gameUI.won after a timeout), so lamp and pulses get about 2 s alone on stage.

The switch then works both ways during the dwell: off → dark → on again. The Meeting projector can keep instant win or use the same dwell.
findings.verify: Playwright: plug in, E (lamp on), then advance(0.5) and assert won===false and electrical==='on'. E again: electrical==='off' and the bulb is unlit (expose a `lampLit` flag in snapshot()). E again, then advance(1.3): won===true. Retake shots 25 and 09: at +0.5 s the bulb is lit with no confetti and no card.
findings.verify_reason: lightUp is only reachable from win() (game.ts:350). The tick calls win() the same frame loads[0] turns on (game.ts:348). win() fires 90 confetti at y=2 over the target and 40 more over Pip (game.ts:351). After that, promptFor returns null (objectives.ts:66) and the driver's live() stops stepping, so the switch can never be turned off again. I reproduced the switch-first path: won:true on the plug-in frame (t 12.78). verify-03 and verify-10 show confetti over the lamp head on frame 0. One correction: the result card lands 1.4 s after the win (game-ui.ts:211-222 setTimeout 1400), not 'about 1 s'.
findings.fix_correction: Same plan, but the extra card delay is optional: the card already waits 1.4 s (game-ui.ts:222). With a 1.2 s dwell, the lamp gets about 2.6 s on screen before the card. The lamp also needs to show its lit/unlit state while the job isn't won yet. Today the only gates are win() and live(), so setLit must be called from step() at game.ts:348, before the won check.

findings.title: The cable reel is shown as the power source: it isn't plugged into anything, the poster says so, and the glowing wall socket next to it is inert
findings.problem:
The reel at (-8,4) stands free in the middle of the floor. No lead runs from it to any wall outlet (game.ts:90-91 builds the drum, axle, foot and spool; decor adds nothing that connects it). The circuit's source `supply` (game.ts:102) is never drawn. The wordless how-to poster on the side wall (decor.ts:98-101; shots 01, 03, 13) reads: yellow reel → orange cable → black plug → teal socket → sun lamp. The reel is the start of the chain.

Meanwhile the back wall has a 'practice wall' of five sockets, one with a green 'live' glow (decor.ts:96-97). It is exactly what a real player would plug a reel into, and the game does nothing with it: carrying the plug there gives 'F Drop the plug' (shot 23).

So the first lesson in an electronics game teaches that a reel (an extension lead) makes electricity. That is the extension-lead version of the well-documented 'battery as current source' / 'source gives out current that gets used' misconception. The reviews cited here (Harvard Project Zero SimpleCircuits, https://pz.harvard.edu/sites/default/files/SimpleCircuits.pdf; Wainwright, https://fg.ed.pacificu.edu/wainwright/Publications/MisconceptionsArticle.06.pdf) report it persisting past school. It breaks AGENTS rule 10 and DR-37 (invisible wiring must be drawn). It also sets up the Meeting, where the reel comes from a 'server closet' with 'the one live outlet', so the two rooms disagree about where power comes from.
evidence: src/levels/decor.ts:96-101 (practice wall with green glow socket; poster starting at the reel)
findings.fix:
Make the supply visible and put it first.

1. In decor.ts playground():
   - Mount a wall outlet plate on the side wall right by the reel, at about (-9.85, .45, 4.0): rbox(.38,.38,.1) with two dark holes.
   - Move the green glow from practice-wall socket k===2 to this outlet, as its 'live' pilot.
   - Draw a short fixed lead (TubeGeometry, radius .05, hose white) from the reel drum (-8,.35,4) to that outlet, ending in a plug seated in it.
2. Change the poster glyph to begin with an outlet icon: outlet → reel → plug → lamp.
3. Either remove the green glow from the practice wall, or let the reel's free plug actually plug into practice-wall sockets (with nothing happening, which is truthful, since a wall socket isn't a load).
4. Optionally put a small flashing breaker on the outlet plate, so the Meeting's breaker isn't the player's first sight of one.
findings.verify: Retake the start and reel close-ups (playground-teach-01, -03) and the survey (-02). The reel's lead visibly ends in a lit wall outlet, and the poster starts at the outlet. A naive viewer asked 'where does the lamp's electricity come from?' points at the wall, not the reel.
findings.verify_reason: The anchor reel (game.ts:90-91) stands free, with no lead to any outlet, and the 'supply' source (game.ts:102) has no mesh. The poster glyph (decor.ts:98-102) begins with the yellow reel circle. The practice wall puts a green glow on socket k===2 (decor.ts:97). The plug-holding prompt only tests distance to level.target (objectives.ts:78), so carrying the plug to that glowing socket gives 'Drop the plug' (reviewer shot 23). Shots 03 and 23 show the free-standing reel and the inert wall sockets. Read at the level taught, an unplugged reel is presented as the source, which is a truthfulness problem (AGENTS 10).
findings.fix_correction: Drop fix step 3's 'let the reel's free plug plug into practice-wall sockets'. That would feed the reel from its own output end, which is electrically meaningless and muddier than the problem it solves. Just remove the green glow from the practice wall, and put the live pilot on the new outlet that the reel's fixed lead runs into.

findings.title: Current pulses run one way on a single hose, and at radius = hose radius they are nearly invisible
findings.problem:
The room's only picture of current is Pulses (src/render/actors.ts:80-86): 4 capsules travelling from the reel to the lamp along the one hose, and only while the load is on (game.ts:304-305).

**What it teaches.** electrical.ts:1-2 says each lead models both conductors and that a missing return is explicit 'rather than teaching a one-wire circuit'. The rendering undoes that. One tube, with slugs moving one way, source to lamp, and none coming back, is the textbook 'current flows to the device and is used up' picture. Licht & Thijs found 61% of 13–14-year-olds hold that view (reported in the misconception reviews: https://fg.ed.pacificu.edu/wainwright/Publications/MisconceptionsArticle.06.pdf). DR-29 and DR-30 require the opposite.

**How it reads.** The capsules have radius .1 (actors.ts:82 default) and the hose has radius .1 (game.ts:304). They are coincident with the hose surface, so they show only as faint white-cyan stripes on the gold cable. In the win shots (10, 29) a single pale slug can be found near the plug. At the game camera the 'current now flows' signal effectively isn't there. With only 4 slugs on an 18 m cable, they are about 4.6 m apart, which makes it worse.
evidence: src/game.ts:304-305 (hose radius .1, pulses on when loads[0] on)
findings.verify: Crop the cable at the game camera 1 s after the lamp lights (with the dwell from the lamp/win finding): at least 6 slugs visible, two lanes moving in opposite directions, at equal spacing either side of the socket. Retake playground-teach-29 and compare.
findings.verify_reason: Pulses (actors.ts:80-86) defaults to count=4 capsules of radius .1, length .4, all moving one way from reel to load. The hose radius is also .1 (game.ts:304), so the slugs are coincident with the tube surface. In verify-11 (2.5 s after the win, no HUD) only a faint white stripe shows near Pip's feet; the reviewer's shot 29 looks the same. electrical.ts:1-2 states that a lead models both conductors, yet the only picture of current is one train going to the lamp, against DR-29 and DR-30.
findings.fix_correction: Offsetting two trains ±0.055 m sideways on a 0.1 m-radius hose puts 0.045 m slugs completely inside the tube, so they would be invisible; polygonOffset/renderOrder can't reveal a mesh enclosed by another. Put the lanes on the surface instead: position = p + up*0.075 ± binormal*0.05, slug radius about 0.035–0.04, so each slug stands out of the hose by about 2 cm. Alternatively draw each lane as a thin emissive stripe in the hose's vertex colours. Keep the rest: reverse train, count ≈ length/1.2, outline.

findings.title: The 'plugged in / live' cable tint is the same hex as the 70–85% strain warning
findings.problem:
game.ts:7 defines `const GOLD=new T.Color('#ffd451')`, the tint for a connected cable (game.ts:304, `tint:this.connected?GOLD:undefined`). sim/cable.ts:83 strainColor uses exactly '#ffd451' for strain 0.7–0.85, the first warning band of AGENTS rule 4's white→yellow→orange→red.

At the moment of plugging in, the cable jumps from orange (strain 0.91, shot 05) to uniform yellow (shot 06), although the strain is still 0.968 (logged at plug-in). The player sees 'the cable relaxed to yellow', when in fact it is nearly at its limit and is now 'live'.

This conflates two concepts the room should keep apart: mechanical strain, and electrical state. It also hides the strain lesson exactly when the cable is taut across the room. The rule set asks for the cable state to read without text (DR-46), and for one meaning per visual (DR-29 for dots, and the same spirit applies to tints).
findings.fix:
Give 'energised' its own channel, separate from strain:
- Keep strain colouring after connection, but have hoseGeometry stop at the strain colour from the plug's last strain, not tint.
- Show 'energised, no current' (plugged in, switch open) as a thin teal (#5ed6cc, the socket-ring colour) stripe or a soft emissive rim along the hose.
- Show 'current flowing' only by the two-lane pulses.

If a gold 'win' state is still wanted, use a clearly different hue (e.g. #f6b93b with a pulsing emissive) that strainColor never produces, and add a unit test asserting GOLD isn't in strainColor's palette.
findings.verify: Unit test in src/sim/cable.test.ts: strainColor outputs never equal the connected tint. Retake shots 05/06: after plug-in, the hose keeps its strain colour, gains a teal stripe, and shows no pulses until the switch closes.
findings.verify_reason: Same hex, confirmed: GOLD '#ffd451' (game.ts:7) is the connected tint (game.ts:304). The hose's own ramp STRAIN uses '#ffd451' at 0.72 (actors.ts:65), and so does strainColor at 0.7–0.85 (cable.ts:83). verify-05 shows the cable orange before plug-in; verify-06 shows it uniform gold afterwards. The claim that this hides a near-limit strain is wrong, though. drawCable uses strain=.3 whenever the plug isn't held (game.ts:294), and rope.pull only acts while holding. A seated plug carries no pull, so the stale rope.strain 0.968 means nothing to the player. What remains is a hue collision (DR-46), which is polish, not P1.
extra_evidence: src/render/actors.ts:65 (STRAIN ramp has #ffd451 at .72 — the ramp actually used by hoseGeometry)
src/game.ts:294 (strain drawn as .3 when plug not held)
findings.fix_correction: Don't keep the plug's last strain after connection; that would paint a slack, seated cable orange or red. After plug-in, draw the normal relaxed ramp (strain .3, white), and show 'live' with a separate cue: a teal stripe or rim, with pulses only when current flows. Alternatively use a connected hue that STRAIN (actors.ts:65) never produces. The unit test should assert the connected tint is outside both STRAIN and strainColor.

findings.title: No moment where the player must apply the idea: three prompts in a row solve the room, and nothing electrical can go wrong
findings.problem:
The clean solve takes 11.9 s of sim time (clean run log). It is: F 'Pick up the plug' → walk → F 'Plug in' → E 'Switch it on'. Each key is named by the pill at the moment it is needed (objectives.ts:72-84), and the card names the next method ('Drag the cable to the lamp's socket and plug it in', 'Switch the lamp on', objectives.ts:24-26).

The circuit can't fail: supply 5 A, lead 3 A, load 1 A (game.ts:102). So there's no wrong electrical choice, and a player who has never heard of a switch succeeds by obeying prompts. The cable-length part is genuinely learned by doing, because a wrong route around pillar-b stalls Pip with a red cable (shot 17), which is good. The electrical part is learned by reading.

This breaks:
- DR-26: the concept should be the act.
- DR-38: trial and error or prompt-following shouldn't be enough.
- DR-39: the goal text should say what, not how ('Switch the lamp on' is the how).
- AGENTS rule 2, play by doing.
evidence: src/game.ts:102 (5 A / 3 A / 1 A, cannot fail)
findings.fix:
With the visible switch (switch finding) and the circuit-driven lamp (lamp/win finding) in place:

1. Merge steps 2 and 3 into one goal, 'Light the lamp'. Drop the 'Switch the lamp on' text, and keep the marker on the lamp, not on the switch.
2. After plugging in, the lamp stays dark and the lever visibly reads OFF. The 'aha' is noticing the open lever. Show the E prompt only within 1.5 m of the lever.
3. Optionally make the loop's gap readable: a clear switch housing in which the open contacts show a visible gap; closing them flashes a spark across (truthful, a small make spark).
4. For a second, optional application, give the lamp post's cord a loose connector at its base that a trainee coworker 'forgot' (open loop in a different place). The bonus 'Find and close every gap' teaches that any break anywhere stops the lamp, which also refutes sequential reasoning.
findings.verify: Blind-play check: hide the prompt pill (CSS) and give a script or human only 'Light the lamp'. Record whether the switch is found without the pill. Update tests/objectives.spec.ts so the card stays 'Light the lamp' after the plug-in, and keep the routes spec green (with the dwell).
findings.verify_reason: The facts hold. Each key is named by the pill (objectives.ts:72-84), and the steps are method-like (objectives.ts:24-26). The circuit can't overload: 5 A supply, 3 A lead, 1 A load (game.ts:102). My clean run solved it by following prompts (plugged at t 12.2, won at 16.3). But this is a Level-00 tutorial under a product-owner override that allows the card and prompt (AGENTS 2), and DR-27 asks for exactly one idea here. DR-38 covers grades and bench tiers, so it is misapplied. The part about the switch being learned by reading is the same problem as findings 0 and 6; on its own this adds little beyond the DR-39 wording.
extra_evidence: AGENTS.md:11 (product-owner override for card + key prompt)
findings.fix_correction: Keep fix steps 1–2: merge steps 2 and 3 into 'Light the lamp', and show the switch prompt only near the lever. Drop step 4, the extra 'find every gap' bonus with a loose connector. It adds a second electrical idea to the first room, which conflicts with DR-27 (one new idea per job).

findings.title: The prompt 'Switch on (needs power first)' is false: the switch works with no power, and order doesn't matter
findings.problem:
Standing at the lamp without the plug, the pill reads 'E Switch on (needs power first)' (objectives.ts:80; shot 14). Pressing E does switch it on (game.ts:217 has no power check). The pill then says 'E Switch it off' (shot 15). If the player then fetches and plugs in the cable, the lamp lights and the job is won on the plug-in frame (run C: won:true at t 9.93 right after F; shot 16).

The physics the game simulates is right: a switch and a plug are two series breaks, and the lamp lights once both are closed, in either order. The wording teaches the opposite: that power has to 'arrive' before a switch can be used. That is the sequential-reasoning misconception ('a change only matters once the current reaches it'), which persists to university level (Harvard SimpleCircuits, https://pz.harvard.edu/sites/default/files/SimpleCircuits.pdf). It breaks AGENTS rule 10 and DR-34 (wording physically right everywhere).
findings.fix: In objectives.ts:80, return {key:'E', text: g.switchedOn ? 'Flip the switch off' : 'Flip the switch on'} regardless of g.connected. The lamp staying dark (with the lamp/win fix) shows that the plug is also needed. If any hint is wanted, put it in the world, not the pill: an unlit outlet pilot on the socket box until the plug is in.
findings.verify: Update tests/objectives.spec.ts with a case that walks to the lamp first and expects 'Flip the switch on', presses E, and expects won===false and switchedOn===true. Then plug in: the lamp lights, and with the dwell, won follows 1.2 s later.
findings.verify_reason: Reproduced. At the lamp without the plug, the pill reads 'E Switch on (needs power first)' (objectives.ts:80). E sets switchedOn=true with no power check (game.ts:217), and the pill changes to 'Switch it off'. Fetching the plug and pressing F wins on that same frame (won:true at t 12.78). The wording implies power has to arrive before a switch matters, which the sim itself contradicts.
extra_evidence: mockups/review5/tools/verify-playground-teach/a.mjs (log: sw:true before plug, won:true on plug frame)
findings.fix_correction: The fix is right. Note that objectives.ts:80 is shared with the Meeting projector, so the new wording ships there too; check tests/objectives.spec.ts for both rooms.

findings.title: The idle route hint uses flowing cyan dots on an open circuit and draws them straight through a crate stack (DR-29 known, confirmed)
findings.problem:
After 35 s without connecting (game.ts:446-448), 40 glowing dots in #9ff3ea ×1.4 (game.ts:100-101) stream from Pip's feet to the socket. The current pulses are cyan #6fe9ff (actors.ts:81): nearly the same colour, the same 'flowing beads' motion, the same meaning to a learner.

They appear while the circuit is open and the plug is lying by the reel (shots 12, 13). So the one picture the game uses for 'current flowing' is shown when no current can flow. That is the exact misconception DR-29 forbids (electricity 'flows to the device' before the loop is closed).

The path comes from detour() over level.obstacles only (the two pillars), so it ignores props. In shot 12 the dotted line runs over the crate stack at about (1,1) and across chairs. It also starts at Pip rather than at the plug, which the player hasn't picked up, so it isn't even the cable's route.
evidence: src/game.ts:446-448 (shown after 35 s while !connected; detour from Pip over pillars only)
findings.fix:
Replace the dots with a non-electrical cue in the route-tape language:
- Yellow #ffc629 floor chevrons (flat boxes .3×.012×.1, rotated along the path), stepping one by one, spaced 0.8 m, with no glow and no motion along the path (or a slow hop), so they can't read as current.
- Start the path at the plug while it isn't held (g.plugPosition), and at Pip only when he holds it.
- Route it with the same obstacles the rope uses (this.obstacles plus the nearby props' AABBs, as in simulateCable), or use the level's first `lanes` polyline (playground.ts:6).
- Delay to 45 s and fade out after 10 s.
findings.verify: Run advance(37) with no input. The screenshot shows yellow chevrons from the reel's plug along the lane, avoiding the crates. No cyan moving beads appear anywhere until loads[0].state==='on'. Grep: no MeshBasicMaterial in a cyan hue except Pulses.
findings.verify_reason: game.ts:100-101 builds 40 MeshBasicMaterial dots, #9ff3ea ×1.4. game.ts:446-448 shows them after 35 s while !connected, along detour(Pip→target, this.obstacles). this.obstacles is only level.obstacles, the two pillars (game.ts:73), whereas the rope also adds furniture (game.ts:280). This is DR-29's own 'Known' item, and it still reproduces. verify-12/13 at t 37 show cyan beads streaming on an open circuit. verify-14 (holding the plug elsewhere at t 41) shows the beads starting at Pip and drawn across a crate and a shelf by the back wall.
findings.fix_correction: Fix the verify grep. The target ring (game.ts:87, #64ddd4) and the ring bursts are static cyan MeshBasicMaterials, so 'no cyan MeshBasicMaterial except Pulses' would fail for the wrong reason. Check instead that no moving bead effect is visible while loads[0].state!=='on'.

findings.title: The objective marker at the lamp sits just under the shade and reads as a second lampshade
findings.problem: The step-3 marker is placed at switchAt, which is the lamp post's base, at y = 2.1 ± 0.18 (objectives.ts:116). The lamp shade is at y 2.55 and the bulb at 2.42 (decor.ts:89-91). The yellow inverted cone ends up nested under the yellow-and-white shade, at the same hue, so at the game camera and close up it looks like part of the lamp: a second, yellow shade (shots 07, 08, 17, 19, 28). The marker 'pointing at the goal' is camouflaged exactly at the goal. This breaks DR-44, which requires the marker to sit above any clutter and read as a marker.
findings.fix: Add an optional `y` (or `h`) to the Step `at()` result. For the playground's lamp step, return {x,z,y:3.3}, or point the marker at the switch lever (about 1.05 m) and place it at lever height + 0.9. Give the marker the ink outline the rulebook asks for (DR-44), and a 2-tone shade (a lighter top).
findings.verify: Retake playground-teach-08 and -28: the marker floats clearly above the shade (or beside the switch), with sky or wall behind it, and is outlined.
findings.verify_reason: The marker sits at the current step's at() at y = 2.1 ± 0.18 (objectives.ts:118; the cited :116 is off by two lines). For step 3 that is switchAt (7.55,-6.35), the post's exact centre (decor.ts:89), so the yellow cone is impaled on the post just under the arm and shade (2.55). In verify-08 it wraps the post like a collar or second shade, and in verify-06/07 it reads as part of the lamp. The marker material also disables its outline (objectives.ts:97 outlineParameters visible:false), which DR-44 explicitly requires.

findings.title: Standing at the plugged-in socket, the prompt offers 'Grab the plant' while the card says 'Switch the lamp on'
findings.problem: After plugging in from the spec's spot, Pip stands about 2.4–3 m from switchAt. nearSwitch uses a 1.9 m radius (game.ts:244), so promptFor falls through to the nearest junk prop: 'E Grab the plant' (shot 28; after the plug-in in the clean run the pill was empty). The card's current step and the key prompt disagree (DR-42), and the plants beside the socket (seeded clutter) compete with the lamp for the player's attention.
findings.fix: In promptFor, when g.connected && !g.switchedOn and the switch is within 3.5 m, return {key:'E', text:'Flip the switch on'} with a direction cue (the marker), before the nearest() fallback. In nearest(), downrank junk while the current step's target is within 3.5 m. Alternatively, keep a 1.5 m clear ring around the lamp in the playground lanes (playground.ts:6, add a lane point at (7.4,-6.1) r 1.6) so no plant sits there.
findings.verify: Plug in with the routes spec, then walk(5.2,-4.2). The pill shows the switch prompt or nothing, never 'Grab the plant'. Add the check to tests/objectives.spec.ts.
findings.verify_reason: Reproduced. After plugging in from the spec spot (5.35,-5.41), which is 2.39 m from switchAt, outside the 1.9 m radius, the pill is empty. After walk(5.2,-4.2) to (5.25,-4.58), the card reads 'Switch the lamp on' while the pill reads 'E Grab the plant', which breaks DR-42.

findings.title: The plug's prongs poke out through the socket box, which is also built twice at the same spot
findings.problem:
On connection, the plug is placed at (target.x,.28,target.z) (game.ts:205), the centre of the socket box. The box is 0.48 × 0.38 × 0.3. The plug mesh (the 'coupler' prefab) is longer than the box is deep, so its two yellow prongs come out of the socket's far face (shots 29 and 26b: two yellow nubs on the dark box's back).

The socket also exists twice: game.ts:88 adds a BoxGeometry(.48,.38,.3) at y .25, and decor.ts:92 adds an rbox(.48,.38,.3,.06) at y .2. That makes two coincident dark boxes, which risks z-fighting and doubles the outlines. Seen up close, the most-watched object in the room looks unfinished.
findings.fix:
1. Delete the plain BoxGeometry socket in game.ts:88 (keep the rounded decor one), or the reverse.
2. Give the socket a front face direction. On connect, place the plug at socket centre + face normal × (0.15 + plugHalfLength − 0.06), so only the prongs enter and the body stays proud of the face.
3. Rotate the plug to face the socket. Add two dark receptacle holes on the face.
findings.verify: After the plug-in, take a zoom-9 crop orbited 180° (g.orbit(±700)): nothing yellow on the socket's back face. Run g.audit(.02) at win: no socket/plug overlap reported.
findings.verify_reason: In the coupler/plug mesh (prefabs.ts:101-102), the body is a 0.3 m cylinder along x, and its prongs are centred at x=.2 with length .14, so the tips reach x=.27. The plug is never rotated (game.ts:293 copies the position only) and is placed at the socket centre (game.ts:205). The socket is 0.48 wide (half-width .24), so the prongs poke about 3 cm out of the +x face. The two yellow nubs are visible in verify-03 and verify-11 and in the reviewer's shots 29 and 26b. The socket is also built twice: game.ts:88 has a BoxGeometry at y .25, and decor.ts:92 has an rbox at y .2, offset by 5 cm, so the outlines double and the shells intersect.

findings.title: Win push-in: the lamp's glow sprite washes Pip into a pale ghost
findings.problem: lightUp() adds glow(…,3,.6), a 3 m sprite at opacity 0.6 at the bulb (decor.ts:93), plus a point light of intensity 10 and a light pool. The win push-in puts the lamp head between the camera and Pip. In shots 10 and 11, Pip shows through a bright cream haze: the outlines are lost, the overalls desaturated, the face barely readable. The success frame is supposed to show Pip and the working machine together (DR-11). Here the 'working machine' is a blown-out blob and Pip is ghosted. This breaks DR-66 (glow ≤ 0.5 opacity, ≤ 1.5× its source, never hiding Pip).
findings.fix: Glow scale 3 → 1.2, opacity .6 → .35, and depthTest true with the bulb sphere as the occluder. Set renderOrder so the sprite draws behind Pip, or fade the sprite while Pip is within 1.5 m of the camera ray. Lower the pointLamp to about 6. In the win push-in (game.ts:369-373 area), bias the playground's push-in yaw so the camera sits on the −x side of the post and the lamp head isn't between camera and Pip.
findings.verify: Retake shot 10: luma of the median Pip-crop pixels within ±15 of the pre-win frame, outline visible all round Pip, bulb readable as a lit bulb under its shade.
findings.verify_reason: decor.ts:93 adds glow(...,3,.6), a 3 m additive sprite at 0.6 opacity on a 0.32 m bulb. That exceeds DR-66's limits of ≤0.5 opacity and ≤1.5× the source. The reviewer's shots 10 and 11 (camera orbited −350 before the win) show Pip ghosted through the haze. The effect depends on yaw: in my default-yaw push-in (verify-11), Pip stays readable and only the area around the lamp is washed. Because the push-in uses the player's current yaw (game.ts:373), the ghosting happens for some approach angles.
findings.fix_correction: Drop 'depthTest true': SpriteMaterial already depth-tests (kit.ts:69). The haze appears because the sprite sits in front of Pip from that yaw, not because depth testing is off. The size/opacity cut (≈0.5 m, ≤0.4) and the push-in yaw bias are the effective parts. Verify with a run that orbits −350 before the win, as clean.mjs does.

findings.title: Spare grabbable reels and splitters from the 'parts' recipe sit around the tutorial room (P6 confirmed)
findings.problem: The Playground's clutter recipes include 'parts' (playground.ts:5). That recipe spawns a grabbable reel and a splitter per cluster (clutter.ts:45). The supply cage also shows two more reels (decor.ts:113). Shot 23 shows a spare reel standing by the back wall. In a room whose lesson is 'this one reel is this long', spare reels and splitters are false affordances (DR-17). A new player tries them as job items ('do I join these?'), and in the very next room (Meeting) joining a second reel really is the clean solution, with a coupler. The tutorial teaches nothing about that join and shows parts it doesn't let you use.
findings.fix: Remove 'parts' from the playground recipe list (playground.ts:5), or add a playground-only variant of it without the reel and splitter (e.g. a toolbox, a cone and a box). Keep the cage reels as non-dynamic decor; they already are. If the room should foreshadow the Meeting, make a locked cage the place for spares.
findings.verify: Survey and start shots: no dynamic `reel`/`splitter` props except the anchor. A scripted check over snapshot items, or a page.evaluate count of props by kind, shows reel count 0 in the playground clutter.
findings.verify_reason: playground.ts:5 includes the 'parts' recipe, which yields a reel and a splitter (clutter.ts:45). Reproduced: at (-3.31,-8.2) by the back wall, the pill offers 'E Grab the splitter' (verify-04). The reviewer's shot 23 shows a spare reel there. These are grabbable job-looking items in a room where they have no use, which breaks DR-17.

findings.title: The playground plug is rendered with the Meeting 'coupler' model, and it is a live male plug going into the load
findings.problem:
The cable's end is makeProp('coupler','#ffcc52') (game.ts:86). The coupler and plug kinds share one mesh (prefabs.ts:101). In the Meeting, a teal 'coupler' is a different job item that joins two reels (objectives.ts NAMES 'coupler'), so the same object means two things (DR-50). It is also a male plug with prongs (shot 29 shows the prongs), and it comes from the energised side. Pip carries a plug that is live as soon as the reel is fed, into a 'lamp's socket' (objectives.ts:25).

In real wiring, the energised side always carries the female connector, so live pins can't be touched. A male-to-male or live-plug arrangement is the notorious 'suicide cord' (https://www.slashgear.com/1859724/suicide-extension-cord-explained-what-happens-plug-in-danger-risks ; the CPSC warning summarised at https://hackaday.com/2022/09/17/the-cpsc-says-plug-to-socket-not-plug-to-plug-please). Lamps have plugs; supplies have sockets. At the game's level the loop still works, but the parts are assigned backwards. That is cheap to fix now and would mislead later, once players see real plugs.
findings.fix:
Swap the gender without changing the mechanic:
1. The reel's free end is a trailing socket: a chunky yellow block with two dark holes, no prongs, and its own prefab kind 'outlet-head'.
2. The lamp gets a short cord from its base ending in a plug that lies on a little stand where the socket box is now.
3. Pressing F at the lamp still 'joins' them, so the snap logic is unchanged.
4. Copy: 'Pick up the cable end', 'Take the cable to the lamp and plug the lamp in'.

If that's too much churn, at minimum give the playground end its own plug mesh distinct from the Meeting coupler, and call the target an 'inlet'.
findings.verify: Close-up retake of playground-teach-22b/-29: no exposed prongs on the carried end, and the prongs on the lamp side seat into the carried head. Grep: the playground no longer uses makeProp('coupler').
findings.verify_reason: game.ts:86 builds the cable end with makeProp('coupler'), and prefabs.ts:101 shares one mesh for 'coupler' and 'plug' (a body plus two prongs). The Meeting's coupler job item has the same NAMES entry, 'coupler' (objectives.ts:58). The carried, energised end is a male plug going into the 'lamp's socket' (objectives.ts:24-25). That reverses the real convention, where the supply side is female and the load has the plug. At the taught level the loop still works, so this is polish, but it is cheap to fix and keeps the parts truthful.

findings.title: Draw calls are about 3× the DR-24 budget at the game camera (782 at start, 948 at win)
findings.problem: snapshot().drawCalls logged 782 at start, 758–800 during the drag, and 948 after the win (clean.mjs log). DR-24 asks for at most about 250 draw calls. It still runs at 60 fps on the host GPU, but a 20×20 m tutorial with at most 90 clutter props shouldn't need 3× the budget the Lunch merge reached (about 175). Low-end machines (the first-run audience of a tutorial) will drop frames during the drag, which is exactly where cable feel matters. Outside my dimension, but measured.
findings.fix: Run the same batchProps/freeze pass used for Lunch over the playground: merge the static decor (cage wires, 18 wire bars, tape, lane lines and shelves) into one geometry per material. Instance the cones, bins and pins. Exclude the win confetti from per-particle meshes, or instance it.

On the same counter, Lunch reads 1297 and Meeting 1314 (verify d.mjs), so 'the Lunch merge reached about 175' isn't comparable, and the playground is the cheapest of the three rooms. By DR-24's literal check it is over 250, but this is a cross-room counter/budget question, not a playground-specific defect. notes.teaching:
The Playground teaches cable feel well, and it does so through play. The 19 m reel over an 18.9 m clean route makes length a real constraint. A wrong route round pillar-b stalls Pip with a red cable and twang arcs at the biting corner (shot 17). The world shows why without printing it. That part meets DR-26 and DR-28.

The electrical idea the room claims ('a switch closes the loop') is not taught by any act or object:
- the switch is an invisible radius at the lamp base;
- its state lives only in the prompt pill;
- the lamp lights only inside win(), under confetti;
- the current pulses are one-way and buried in the hose;
- the reel itself is shown as the source of electricity.

The one prompt that addresses order ('needs power first') teaches sequential reasoning. Nothing electrical can fail (5 A / 3 A / 1 A), so the room can be solved by obeying three prompts without learning anything about circuits.

What is truthful already: the simulation is a series condition (the plug AND the switch must both be closed, in either order). The pulses only run on a closed, live loop. The game also distinguishes 'plugged in' from 'on'. The fixes are almost all in presentation, plus one in sequencing (the dwell and win decoupling). Recommended order:
1. Visible switch with lever state.
2. Circuit-driven lamp with a 1.2 s dwell before the win.
3. Visible wall supply feeding the reel.
4. Two-lane loop pulses that can actually be seen.
5. Non-electrical idle hint.
6. Fix the prompt wording.
7. Separate the live tint from strain yellow.
notes.fun: The slingshot remains the best toy, and the tension tagline lands. Overstretching makes coworkers alarm with '!' bubbles, props fly (fastestProp 44 m/s), and damage and cost tick on the HUD (shots 19–21). The scripted slingshot from tests/routes.spec.ts knocked a plant and a chair, not the pins (pinsDown 0 in runs D and E), so the bowling bonus needs a deliberate aim. That is fine for a bonus, but the spec comment's 'front row of boxes' no longer matches where the cable lies. The win itself is a confetti burst that happens too fast to enjoy the lit lamp. A 1–2 s 'it works!' beat before the card would make the payoff land and double as the teaching moment.
notes.playability: Controls behaved as prompted in every state I drove: F pick up, F plug, E switch, Q slingshot, F drop. No console or page errors in four scripts (every g.close() returned []). When Pip is stuck short on a wrong route, the only prompt is 'Q Let go to slingshot the cable'. A learner gets told the chaos option, not that the route is too long. Consider letting the strain HUD meter or the reel spool pulse instead. Draw calls are about 780–950 (P2 finding). The plug-snap radius (2.2 m from Pip) is forgiving and worked first time at the spec point. A strain ≥ 1.12 plug-in rejection (game.ts:205) exists, but I couldn't reach it near the socket (max observed strain about 1.045), so I don't report it.
